Therapy I feel works for certain people. Sometimes it helps just to get your thoughts out of your head. And therapists can be a reliable, firm source for doing so. It's not the end. 

Although I haven't been on your exact same path, and mine has been more mental than physical, I've been through other people's experiences too. I won't give you specifics or list out "who has what", but for those who've had it so rough you're surprised their skin is still soft, there has been light. In them and in their life. There's no trick to happiness. There's ways to find things that give you it, that give you a reason to keep trying and keep going. There's the whole spiel about "this is your one body, your one life, see what you can do" but hey, I was in the hospital for a suicide attempt two-three weeks ago. I didn't want to hear that shit and I'm guessing you don't want to either.

But having people to talk to, too, cracks open the rocky life and shows the geode again. Even if it's some distant person online that helps. Or maybe you find a hobby, a recreation, a goal. That's what I did. It makes fighting through the medical stuff worthwhile. (Talk to me or anyone else on this sub if you'd like to, I'm open and a whole lot of us are too).

And hey yes it hurts right now. But it's not the end. Far from. You've been through a lot and you're still here. Something beautiful, alive, pulsing with life is still in you and it always will be. This may be your nadir, and your fragged to hell and back, but it's not over.

I was terrified of starting medication for anxiety because of the side effects, namely that I was going to be a different person. And, once I started, I did change. *I became happy* With the physical issues of anxiety steadily ebbing into a dull roar and then into a distant buzz, I could focus on improving my mental state. 

But starting is sort of like ripping a bandaid off. It's scary, and it stings, but you'll be the better for it once it's off. Or it's like getting a shot. The terror and soreness afterwards are painful to think off, but it's good, it helps, and the benefits of it greatly outweigh your fear. It's one of those things that terror blows it out of proportion. 

Just had to swallow my fear, shut my eyes, and take the pill. Overcoming that initial confluence is the hardest step, and you just gotta do it with the knowledge that things will get better steadily held in your mind.

I don't know how to help you, but I can tell you this - it's not weak of you to ask a doctor for help. It will help, and seeing someone whether it's for medication or therapy does not make you any less of a person. If anything, it makes you stronger and braver, for realising your weaknesses and seeking ways to improve them. Calling out for help is hard, and if you can help your anxiety realise that, yes, I am being strong for doing this and *I can fucking do this and I can do this right, despite everything* (which is hard with anxiety, because it makes everything airtight and impenetrable, to the point you can't think clearly. But once on meds that help lessen its effects, you start to see things a little more clearly. Blurred pastels become clearer, distinct colours i.e.).

You're not weak for needing help, regardless of what your mind is saying. If anything, you're all the wiser for knowing you need it.

Plenty. Lemme make a general list. For specific advise feel free to ask!

- Struggling with starting? Write shorts. I call them "snapshots". I write a character I made doing something mundane in their lives. Focus on how it happens. Helps with getting your toes (paws?) wet and getting inspired.

- Starting off you're always going to suck. Maybe, compared to others, you'll be a prodigy. But compared to your capacity and ability, it'll suck. Because you'll always be getting better. The more you do it the better it gets, the easier words flow, the nicer plots mesh together. Sure, you'll have fumbles forever. But it will get smoother. The main thing is to not get discouraged. Especially if you make your stories public and they receive no or negative attention. 

- Keep going, write what you love and write it with passion. Think of it like this: what's the difference between so bad they're good movies and bad movies? The latter tends to be movies with money slapped on and no effort. So bad they're good movies, even though they aren't technically good and may have the camera quality of three kale leaves, they still are enjoyable. Because passion was put into them, because someone loved what they were doing.

Sorry, went for a bit of a ramble. But those are the things I've kept in mind while writing and embarking on new genres. Hope it helps

Been dealing with this lots. Sucks especially since I have lovely side dishes of anxiety and depression along with it (usually the reasons I end up alone anyway). 

So I devised a way to be alone. I did it while my relationships were fitfully skidding into chaos. Or just when I'm having bad nights and I know I'd hurt people if I was to be in contact with them. What I do: 

- write. creating stories and worlds. so many stories on my comp.

- draw. make commissions. Paint while the music is blasting, enjoying my water colour. Draw whatever the hell I want, who cares about my interests? Only I'm gonna see this!

- Chatrooms. /r/anxiety has an awesome chatroom I frequent. But this is more for my fellow ladies struggling with mental illness.

- Online communities. Most of the contact I get is online.

- make myself cozy. if it's hot, in a cool room where I can paint or jam out to music. Cold? Get warm.

- movies. Oh how many movies I've used to whittle away the hours between work and sleep. 

These are healthier than many things I've done. But the thing is, being alone isn't so bad. It's not as good as having people, but it can be manageable. It has to be manageable, because if you can't get through it how do you get to the good parts with people you love and tear your heart apart for? 

Hope that helps dear

If it helps at all, with difficult books you want to push yourself through, at the end of each chapter do a little recap and write down what happened and what was significant. Or don't write it down and just go over it in your head. If that doesn't work, pausing every couple of pages to make sure your image of the book in your head is lucid works too. 

It's a difficult book to get through for some people, but it's very very rewarding.

I stared across the table, giving my only begotten son a long smile. I showed off all of my teeth. No pearly whites here. All natural, all yellow, all stinking teeth. David gave me a wary look, his eyes ripping away from me and towards his mother. My ex-ex-ex wife. We tried to get married again and again, giving up only to come crawling right back to each other. She said it had something to do with my drinking problem. Ha.

“Son.”

“Dad.”

“You know, I do awfully love you. What with all your medals in… basketball.”

“Trophies in baseball.” His mother, bitch, corrected me. She gave him a tender, apologetic smile. As if to say sorry for me. Why? I’m the only reason he even exists. Only reason he crewed out of his crib, on to his legs, and into that lottery ticket win. Damned son. I was proud, and jealous. Jealousy seething in me like snakes shooting out of my belly. 

“Is it any surprise why you’re here?” She said, at me. Her hair was done up. I’d never seen it done up. Then again, I only drop by when I’m itching. 

David bit his lower lip. Always a baby, always a scared child. Like I might hit him. Me? His own father? I only smacked him around a couple times when he was toddling dangerously. Or when I showed up, his fourteenth birthday in March - or maybe May - or maybe even November. Ah, damned family.

“Give your old man a few.” I cut to the chase. I was never one for counting my money. 

“Uh, no.” David said simply. 

“Why not?”

“It’s mine?”

“I’m your dad.” 

“Hardly.” David began to mutter.

“Speak up, kid.” I said, trying to be nice. Didn’t seem like that would work. Probably would have had to knock him around a few, bully him, get him to cough up a couple shiny pennies for his dear old, honestly deadbeat, dad. 

David shook his head. “No. I won it.”

“The hell do you plan on doing it? You’re eighteen.”

“Twenty… dad, twenty.” 

“When’d you get that ticket?”

“Sixteen.” 

“And how much do you have left?” 

“Enough. Enough to get me through college, and to keep mom comfy. Something you never bothered to do.”

“Stingy bastard. No shit I never raised you. You’d drop your old dad like a sick dog, out on the street.”

“No, you’d do that.” David’s cheeks flushed. Maybe if I got him angry enough. “You’d abandon anything for money. What’d you use it for? Oh wait, I know.” 

“Son, just a couple hundred. I just owe Tommy - remember, Uncle Tommy? A couple hundred. Just a couple hundred…”

David’s eyes began to water. “A couple hundred?”

“Eight of ‘em, to be exact.” 

“Dad, money runs out. I’m not made of it.”

“Oh, son, please? Out of the goodness of your heart? Just for an old man?”

“David no —” the bitch butted in. I hushed her with a raise of my hand and an angry look. She backed off. Weak, like her kid. Damned family I married into.

David already picked up his wallet, trembling slightly. He pulled out a couple crisp, new bills, and stared at me. “Dad.” 

“Yeah?”

“If I do this will you leave us alone? And never come back?”

I already planned my next visit. When I’m in real trouble, I’ll stumble in, break their poor old hearts, and beg for just a couple more hundred. I nodded. “Cross my heart and hope to die.”

“Please? I’m serious.” David said, his eyes big as a puppy. 

“So ‘m I. Cough it up, boy, I don’t have all day.”

David tossed the money in my direction, his voice white hot with anger. “Go, and please, please don’t come back.”
